title: Foxes, Fire, and the Jawbone of a Donkey
summary: Denied his wife, Samson burns the Philistines' grain, vineyards, and olive groves by releasing torch-bearing foxes, and the Philistines retaliate by burning his wife and her father. After a cycle of revenge, three thousand men of Judah bind Samson and hand him over, but the Spirit rushes upon him, the ropes melt away, and he kills a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone. Dying of thirst, he calls on the LORD, who opens a spring, and the chapter closes by noting he judged Israel twenty years.
story: Chapter 14 ended with Samson's bride given to his companion and Samson returning home in anger. Chapter 15 follows the consequences in an escalating spiral of reprisal, each side paying the other back. What began as a personal grievance becomes a regional crisis, and Judah, rather than rallying to Samson, hands him over to keep the peace with their overlords. The chapter's turning point is Samson's first recorded prayer, a cry of need at the edge of death. It marks one of the few moments when Samson acknowledges that his strength and victory come from God. The closing note that he judged Israel twenty years gives the chapter a sense of summary, though chapter 16 will tell how his story ends.
historical:
The Philistine domination of Israel described in 13:1 is visible here in Judah's attitude. The men of Judah say plainly that the Philistines rule over them, and they fear what Samson's actions will provoke. Judah, the largest southern tribe, had been the first to fight in 1:1-2 and had taken significant territory, but now it has accepted subjection. Lehi, meaning jawbone, was a place in Judah whose exact location is unknown. The rock of Etam was likewise in Judah; an Etam near Bethlehem is mentioned in 2 Chronicles 11:6, but whether it is the same place is uncertain.

The wheat harvest in the region came in late spring and early summer, around May and June. Setting fire to fields of ripe grain at that season destroyed a year's food supply, along with the vineyards and olive groves that were the region's other major crops. For an agrarian people this was a grave economic blow.
cultural:
Revenge was an accepted part of honor culture in the ancient Near East: an insult or injury to a family required a response, and the response invited another. Samson's words in 15:3, 15:7, and 15:11 show this logic plainly: he is paying back what was done to him. The Philistines' burning of his wife and her father carries out the threat they had made in 14:15, a grim irony. Israel's law sought to limit revenge by placing justice in the hands of courts and restricting retaliation to proportionate penalties (Exodus 21:23-25), but the chapter shows vengeance running without restraint.

The Hebrew word translated foxes (shu'al) can also refer to jackals, which roam in packs and would have been easier to catch in number; interpreters differ on which animal is meant. A fresh jawbone would be heavy and strong, unlike an old, brittle one, which is why the text notes it. Contact with a dead animal's remains is not directly forbidden to Nazirites in Numbers 6 (the law concerns human corpses), but repeated contact with death through carcass and killing is a thread in Samson's story that raises questions about how seriously he took his consecration.
literary: The chapter is built on retaliation, with the phrase of doing to someone as they did to you recurring. Each act of violence answers the last: the stolen bride, the burned fields, the burned family, the great slaughter, the Philistine raid on Judah, the binding, and the thousand killed. Samson's victory song in 15:16 is a play on words in Hebrew, where the word for donkey (chamor) sounds like the word for heap (also chamor). It is his own boast, and he doesn't mention God. The reversal comes in 15:18, where he calls on the LORD and admits the deliverance was God's. Place names are explained at the end, as often in the Old Testament, with Ramath-lehi (hill of the jawbone) and En-hakkore (spring of the one who called) recording the two sides of the story: Samson's strength and his dependence.

outline.t: Samson's wife given away, and his vow of revenge
The foxes and the fields, the Philistine reprisal, and Samson's revenge
Judah binds Samson and hands him over
The Spirit rushes upon him, and the jawbone victory
Samson's thirst, his prayer, and the spring at Lehi

doctrines.note: Samson's first recorded prayer comes when he is at the end of his strength. God answers a cry of need even from someone whose life has been self-directed, and the place name keeps the memory of that calling out.
Again the Spirit rushes upon Samson, and bonds fall away. The Spirit's empowerment for deliverance is real even when the man is flawed, and the victory is the LORD's.
The chapter shows how private grievance escalates into cycles of violence that consume the innocent. Revenge produces more revenge, and no one in the story is able to break the pattern.

words.note: Lechi, jaw or jawbone, used four times and also as the place name Lehi. The word ties the victory to the place, and the chapter plays on it repeatedly. It also underlines the strangeness of the weapon: an unclean, improvised tool in the hand of a Nazirite.

Naqam, to avenge or take vengeance, used in 15:7. The word can describe God's just vengeance on evil or human retaliation. Samson uses it of his personal revenge. In the law and the prophets, vengeance ultimately belongs to God (Deuteronomy 32:35), and this chapter shows why that is a mercy.

Teshu'ah, deliverance, salvation, or victory. In 15:18 Samson calls the jawbone victory a great deliverance that the LORD accomplished through his servant. It is the first time Samson credits God, and the word links his personal fight to Israel's larger need for rescue.

Shava, to swear an oath. Samson makes the men of Judah swear not to kill him themselves (15:12). Oaths bound people before God, and Samson trusts their oath even as they hand him over, a detail that shows how far Judah's loyalty had shifted.

christ: Two patterns in this chapter find echoes in the gospel, though neither is a direct prophecy. First, Samson is bound by his own people and handed over to the Gentile rulers to keep the peace, as Jesus was bound by the leaders of his own nation and delivered to Pilate (Mark 15:1). The difference is that Samson breaks free and slaughters his enemies, while Jesus allowed himself to be led away and prayed for those who crucified him (Luke 23:34). Second, Samson is saved by water springing from the ground when he calls on God. Jesus himself cried out in thirst on the cross (John 19:28), and he promised living water to those who ask him (John 4:10). The link is thematic: God provides life to those at the end of their strength.

hard.q: Why does Scripture include such a cycle of revenge, and does God endorse Samson's violence?
hard.a: The chapter narrates the violence without making it a model. Samson's motive is plainly personal revenge, and he says so. The Philistines' burning of his wife is brutal, and his slaughter in response is disproportionate. The narrator neither praises nor condemns directly, a common practice in Judges, which lets the reader see the consequences. At the same time, the Spirit of the LORD rushes upon Samson in 15:14, and God answers his prayer in 15:19. Interpreters hold these together in different ways. Some stress that God was using Samson's actions to begin Israel's deliverance from Philistine rule, as 13:5 and 14:4 promised, and that the empowering Spirit shows God's purpose despite Samson's motives. Others emphasize that the narrator's silence invites moral judgment, and that Samson's story shows what happens when a leader's gift is not matched by character. Both readings recognize that the Bible describes much it does not approve.

questions: The phrase of doing to others what they did to you drives this chapter. Where do you see cycles of retaliation in families, communities, or nations, and what could break them?
The men of Judah handed over their deliverer to keep the peace with their oppressors. When is keeping the peace actually a failure of courage or loyalty?
Samson called on the LORD only when he was about to die of thirst. What does it take for you to recognize your dependence on God?
